title: Been working on my cozy cyberpunk city builder for the last three months. Here's the teaser trailer for it! Free to play on itch.io and would love to hear what you think.
author: senpai_go_away
selftext:
Neon Terrarium is essentially something my friend wanted, which was Townscaper but cyberpunk. I was looking for a new project to immerse myself in, and game dev was something I always kinda wanted to get into (back when RPG Maker was a thing). So I thought I'd give it a shot with AI. It's still being built, but I mostly have the fundamental mechanics down.  

Every building is generated procedurally with there being four zones/sectors you can choose to build from. All the npcs have a storylet engine driving them with jobs, relationships, and drama as well. Crime is also a part of the storylet engine, with cops on the (possible) hunt for a drug lord. Essentially, there is always a crime story running and cops have a certain chance of stumbling upon it, and depending on when they stumble upon it affects their chances of solving it. There are megastructures to unlock (currently have 15 in the game). You can also furnish all the apartments in the game, and all apartments are procedurally furnished based on who's living in the apartment and their personality traits. Something pretty cool is there's a Jam Booth as well, where you can kinda make your own music or remix some of your favourite songs. Happy to explain more about anything if you're interested!

If you'd like to play, you can check it out here: [https://jannstudios.itch.io/neon-terrarium](https://jannstudios.itch.io/neon-terrarium)  
Works on both browser and mobile too (Just had a big update to improve UI and performance for mobile).

Would be super grateful to get some feedback and just hear what you think! Happy to answer any and all questions too!

Often, a lot of anti AI game devs and people who do want to use AI to build games and put the effort to do it, are saying the same thing, which is, put in effort to do what you want to do, don't just push something out because you can. I also do understand where they are coming from. Generative AI is, at best, controversial, when addressing the ethics of where a lot of the data has been pulled from without the consent of artists and developers. Someone who has taken years to build the knowledge and skills to do something, only to be incorrectly told that AI can do what they do and better would make anyone feel pretty hostile. It's a tricky and not a particularly enviable place for people wanting to use AI to be in.

comments.author: Kiko_Production
comments.body: How did you optimize your game to handle a large number of townspeople and their behavior?

replies.author: dataoops
replies.body: "claude this shit is slow can you make it support more people please"

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body:
First off, great question. Second, GOD IT WAS A ABSOLUTE NIGHTMARE. I've come out of the other side with so much more empathy for unoptimised games and in awe of traditional game devs who've had to do this on their own. So, breaking it down:  
  
The people and behaviour actually takes very little to do. Everytime an npc is spawned in, they have a seed which dictates all of their traits, where they'll live, where they'll work etc. So, there's no real processing overhead for this since it happens once in the beginning. You don't really have to check their behavior every frame and most of the pathfinding and stuff is not really intensive. the NPCs themselves are tiny 2d sprites which means no gpu load for draw calls either.

The trick to the storylet engine is that the game has a surveillance cam. You can select any npc and then watch them. After a predetermined amount of time, the game realises you're invested in this NPC, and then begins their storylet. You can also save NPCs in the game, and if you do that, the game runs their storylet in the background. Watchdog legions was the inspiration for this, they did something similar where you could look at any NPC and they'd have a life they were living.

The real struggle was actually just the buildings. The game has a lot of lighting and other effects, combined with just the sheer number of geometry on the screen at scale, it really was a struggle to get this going. Ended up learning a couple of neat little tricks. If you're interested, happy to elaborate more.

Hope I answered your question and thank you for stopping by!

replies.author: elimit
replies.body: I’d love to hear those tricks regarding the geometry optimizations. This looks amazing

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body:
I'd love to tell you! So, first, claude, and most AIs (from what I hear) tend to be pretty generous with polygon counts when making assets, so the first step is generally a simple prompt of asking it "without making any significant visual changes, reduce polygon count for the assets." This generally means, no random surfaces in the interior of the building that no one will ever see, complex shapes that don't need to be complex etc. That would be step 1.  
Then, you start baking most of the details as textures with depth maps. So, the windows and the small detail on the surfaces of the building aren't built using any geometry (Doom Eternal does this, in fact, I found out about this by looking up how Doom ran so smoothly despite looking so visually intensive).  
Then you use basic cost saving measures like LODs (level of detail, which means the further away you are, the less it will render), and Occlusion Culling, where if the camera can't see the surface, you don't render it, so back of the buildings won't render if the camera can't see them.  
The big cheat (and probably the biggest pain point) was using a cache for the city. The isometric camera view meant that, you generally were looking at it from a fixed angle. So, we essentially take a 2D photo of the city, use a bunch of depth maps and lighting tricks and render that. If you pan, it just pulls in that section that you're panning towards in slices. If you rotate, the cache stops rendering and it switches to 3D again. However when you rotate, the camera is in motion, so we can get away with a lower LOD since you can't see much anyway. That's mostly how I get away with getting all of this to run smoothly. There are issues, like rotating slowly means no lowering of LOD and rendering the whole city in 3D. You try to kinda cheat your way through that too by rendering parts of the city in the distance with a lower LOD and having parts in the distance move a little quicker so you can't tell. When you build a new building or the city, the cache needs to update. Since there is a day night cycle, you save the cache with a depth map attached to it so you can fake the lighting. I think this mostly covers it.

Let me know if there's anything else you'd like to know or if I can clear anything else up. Thank you for your question!

comments.author: ArthursoftDev

Just had a little play around, it's got a heck of a lot of charm, although the iso/fov stretched look really hurts my brain 👀. I'm really interested in your process and tech stack, what AI models? how where the assets created? What does your iteration process look like?

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body:
Thank you so much for playing, and gosh, thank you for the kind words. Could you please help me with a little more detail on the FOV issue? I'd love to fix it, just not really sure what to adjust. Does it feel too restrictive? Too wide?

Okay, so nothing fancy at all, just claude with opus 5.5. Assets were created with claude too, literally didn't use anything apart from that for the game. So asset generation. The way I went about it was I first created a mood board using pinterest and meta's image generator. Then, I started searching for an art style and t3ssel8r's visual motifs and aesthetics looked really cool to me. I essentially asked claude to help me break down the style, then used that as inspiration to create my own pixel art toon shader. Meta made the buildings based on what I prompted it to and then claude used it as a reference and built it in the art style. It did take a lot of iterations, and was a relatively slow process. I think it's best to think of yourself as an incompetent game director who has a ton of talented people working for you. You don't really know what you want, and they can only provide you with what you can verbalize. So it's just a process of getting something back, doing your best to remove things you don't like and add things you think would look cool and so on.

If I'm being honest, I do think the assets themselves are pretty generic. What makes the look is the lighting, which I spent a ton of time on. I had several boards on pinterest which were heavily curated for the color and feel they gave. A great way to check this out is that the city settings in the game (not the settings on the top right, the settings near the build zones) has an advanced tab where you can mess with the look and lighting of the game. Change it up and you'll see the assets while cute, lose a lot of their appeal under the wrong lighting. Since I lacked any traditional game dev experience, I used what I kinda know, which was a little photography. It's rarely the subject itself that catches your eye, it's how you frame it and how you color correct it. That's what really makes a photo come alive (imo). 

I hope that somewhat answers your question? Let me know if there is anything else I can clear up!

replies.author: ArthursoftDev
replies.body:
That's really interesting that it was just Claude that's been making the models, it's been really hit and miss for me when making props in our game (which was why I ended up going down more of a 2D mode 7 route).  
  
Like, sure the models themselves are still simple, but imho you've managed to squeeze a lot of charm with the various layered effects.  
  
I wouldn't call the isometric camera/FOV thing a "problem" it's just how isometric camera's work which is great when you're head on or at 45 degree angles. but off that it always looks weird to me.

(red line where you'd instinctively expect the right edge to be after looking at the left edge)

https://i.redd.it/qs96noma21zh1.png

Could maybe look at snapping into an isometric camera when head on/at 45 degrees and then use a Persective camera at other times? Not a huge deal, just reminded me of how things look in CAD/DCC tools with perspective off.

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body:
Thank you for those nice words! All AI, I truly lack the artistic ability to do any of this by hand. I mentioned this in a little more detail in another comment, but I essentially used a ton of references for the tone and vibe I wanted to go for before I even began the asset generation process. Generally the KISS (Keep It Simple Stupid) approach really works for AI in my opinion. The issue is a lot gets lost in trying to convey a feel or a vibe or an aesthetic without a visual reference and so mood boards that you take time to curate (pinterest was my choice) really do help the AI to garner a sense of what you have in your head. So, the mood board didn't always have buildings in it, sometimes it was just a rainy noir street, sometimes it was a movie poster. But all of it conveyed the feel I wanted, and I think once those reference images were provided it did a really good job understanding what I wanted from it.

I think after the mood board and after giving it a pretty concrete reference for an art style, asset generation should improve significantly. Does that help/answer your question? Happy to clarify any questions you may have.

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body:
¡Gracias! Estoy usando una herramienta de traducción, así que pido disculpas si surge alguna dificultad para entender el mensaje.

El tráiler se creó, en esencia, desarrollando una parte independiente del juego que eliminaba cualquier elemento aleatorio propio de la generación procedimental; cada acción estaba estrictamente guionizada. Definí cada escena con gran precisión —incluyendo lo que ocurría en ella, el entorno, el movimiento de los PNJ y la hora del día—, cuidando hasta el más mínimo detalle.

Gran parte del resultado fue posible gracias a que todo se ejecutó directamente dentro del motor del juego; además, dediqué mucho tiempo a asegurar que el juego, por sí mismo, tuviera un buen aspecto. Si hay algo más que te gustaría saber, ¡no dudes en preguntar!

comments.author: Warlaw
comments.body: This game looks so cool! How do you structure the codebase and your prompts so the AI keeps context as the project grows? Do you keep a design doc, an architecture file, or a running summary you feed back in?

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body: Hey! Thank you for stopping by! Claude projects and different threads for different things was the main way I went about it. I had a repo and claude is pretty good at referencing it, and it often makes its own comments so it knows what to check. I don't really think I had an issue with context loss, but I did use claude opus 5.5 and I've found does a great job of indexing the things it needs to remember. Hope that helps? Let me know if there's anything else I can clarify for you!

replies.author: Warlaw
replies.body: Thanks, that’s helpful! Since you split work across different threads, how do you catch it when a change in one area breaks something that was working in another? Do you have any automated tests, or is it mostly play testing?

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body: So generally, the game systems don't really interact in a way where on thing breaks the other. Well, I guess, that depends on your definition of "breaks". For example, when I added the Maglev Metro and had an elevator system for it, NPCs were too big and clipped through. I only found this out through playtesting. Like, systems were rarely perfect, and once vibe-coded in, almost always had an issue that you'd find once you play test. But like, I don't think I ever had anything where an entire gameplay mechanic stopped working because of some other system not working. That's probably also because the game doesn't have a massive scope for that to happen. Most systems run pretty independently. If you're curious about a particular system, feel free to ask and I'll do my best to answer.

replies.author: Warlaw
replies.body: Fascinating! The only other thing I can think of if bug testing. How do you describe a bug to the AI? I've tried a bunch of things like screenshots, clips and the like but with mixed results. Thank you so much for taking the time to answer these questions! You rock!

replies.author: senpai_go_away
replies.body: I think a bit of everything you mentioned, plus how I was able to recreate it. So, what works for me is letting the LLM know exactly what I did in game to get it to bug out along with any visual references. Since this is a browser game, I'd sometimes ask claude to debug my browser and "watch" me play as I recreated the bug. That almost always pointed it in the right direction to solve the issue. Hope that helps!

I've done a small write up on what I did in a comment that was asking a similar question. Feel free to read through and ask any questions you may have!
